At least two reflex corners are excluded
Large-N low-threshold stationary polygons are convex

proofs.proof_text: By @def-stationary-polygon, the derivative of \(J=A\lambda\) vanishes for every vertex displacement. Hadamard’s formula is \[ DJ[V]=A\int_{\partial P}(c-q)V\cdot\nu\,ds. \] Moving one endpoint of an effective edge while keeping the other fixed produces an affine normal velocity on that edge, and the two endpoint velocities give the independent functions \(1\) and \(s/\ell_E\). Since adjacent effective edge normals are linearly independent at a genuine corner, stationarity forces both coefficients of these two affine test functions to vanish. Rescaling \(s/\ell_E\) gives the displayed moments.

Define the divergence-free stress tensor \[ T=
abla u\otimes

abla u|^2-\lambda u^2)I. \] An Airy potential \(\psi\) with \(D^2\psi=R^TTR\) exists locally and, after setting \(\Phi=\psi-c|x|^2/4\), satisfies \[ D^2\Phi=	frac12(|
abla u|^2+\lambda u^2-c)I-
abla u\otimes
abla u. \] Every boundary segment is effective by @def-admissible-polygon, so the identities in @lem-edge-moments apply on each segment. The planar Airy-potential theorem for a symmetric divergence-free stress on the simply connected polygon supplies one global \(\psi\), unique up to an affine function. The two moments imply that \(
abla\Phi\) has the same endpoint values on each segment. Propagating around the boundary and subtracting an affine function makes \(\Phi=0\) at every vertex and \(\partial_
u\Phi=0\) on every segment; the mixed Hessian term vanishes there as well. At a corner of angle \(\omega<2\pi\), the leading Dirichlet mode is \(r^\alpha\sin(\alpha	heta)\) with \(\alpha=\pi/\omega>1/2\), hence \(|
abla u|=O(r^{\alpha-1})\), \(|
abla\Phi|=O(r^{2\alpha-1}+r)\), and \(|D^2\Phi|=O(r^{2\alpha-2}+1)\). These estimates make the circular boundary flux \(O(\varepsilon^{4\alpha-2}+\varepsilon^{2\alpha})	o0\).Apply the divergence identity \[ \operatorname{div}\{\Delta\Phi
abla\Phi-D^2\Phi
abla\Phi\}=(\Delta\Phi)^2-|D^2\Phi|^2 \] to \(P\) with corner disks removed and let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). The edge terms vanish by the preceding boundary conditions, hence \(\int_P\det D^2\Phi=0\). The eigenvalues of \(D^2\Phi\) are \((\lambda u^2-c\pm|
abla u|^2)/2\), so expanding their product and using \(\int_Pu^2=1\) gives the stated identity.

The domain-independent Dirichlet heat-kernel estimate gives \(\|u\|_\infty^2\le e^2\lambda/(8\pi)\) for the normalized first eigenfunction. Under the edge-moment hypotheses, @lem-airy-identity applies, and \(\int_Pu^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\int_Pu^2=\|u\|_\infty^2\); combining these facts yields \[ \int_P|\nabla u|^4\le \frac{e^2\lambda^3}{8\pi}. \] The same \(L^\infty\) bound gives \(\int_P|u|^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\), so the \(W^{1,4}(P)\) norm is bounded by a constant depending only on \(A_0\) and \(\Lambda\). Since \(u\in H^1_0(P)\), its zero extension has no boundary distribution term in its weak gradient; the extension therefore lies in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) with the same gradient bound. Morrey’s inequality in dimension two then gives a \(C^{0,1/2}\) representative with the same parameter dependence.

By @def-conformal-data, \(g\) is analytic, has no constant or linear coefficient, and satisfies \(S=\|g\|_{A^2}^2\); its normalized conformal pullback is the weighted disk problem used below. Put \(d(z)=1-|z|\). The Green kernel of the disk satisfies \[ |
abla_xG_D(x,z)|\le C|x-z|^{-1}, \qquad |
abla_xG_D(x,z)|\le C rac{d(z)}{|x-z|^2}. \] The Bergman pointwise estimate gives \(|g(z)|\le C\|g\|_{A^2}/d(z)\) for \(g\in A^2\) with vanishing constant coefficient. If \(h\in X\), then \(|h(z)|\le d(z)\|h\|_X\). Splitting the Green integral into \(|x-z|<d(x)/2\), the annulus \(d(x)/2\le|x-z|<2d(x)\), and dyadic outer annuli, the two kernel bounds give \[ \|G_D(gh)\|_X\le C\|g\|_{A^2}\|h\|_X, \qquad \|G_D(g_1\overline{g_2}h)\|_X\le C\|g_1\|_{A^2}\|g_2\|_{A^2}\|h\|_X. \] For example, in the near region \(d(z)\simeq d(x)\) and the pointwise bounds leave an integrable \(|x-z|^{-1}\) kernel; in the outer annuli \(d(z)\le d(x)+|x-z|\) cancels one power of the second Green bound, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\|g_1g_2\|_{L^1}\le C\|g_1\|_{A^2}\|g_2\|_{A^2}\). Polynomial approximation extends these estimates to all \(A^2\) data, and the Green potential has a continuous boundary derivative.Define the real quadratic compact-operator family \[ K_g h=G_D[|1+g|^2h]=G_D[h+2\operatorname{Re}(g)h+|g|^2h] \] onlinearly in \(g\). The estimates give \(\|K_g-K_0\|_{B(X)}\le C(\sqrt S+S)\). The operator \(K_0\) is compact on \(X\) by disk Poisson regularity and the compact embedding \(C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{\mathbb D})\Subset C^1(\overline{\mathbb D})\). Its nonzero eigenvalues are the reciprocals of the Dirichlet eigenvalues; \(1/j^2\) is an isolated simple eigenvalue.Choose a fixed small contour \(\Gamma\) enclosing only \(1/j^2\). For \(S\) small, the Neumann series uniformly bounds \((zI-K_g)^{-1}\) on \(\Gamma\) and defines the rank-one Riesz projection \[ \Pi_g= rac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma(zI-K_g)^{-1}\,dz. \] The normalized vector \[ \widetilde v(g)=\Pi_gv_0, \qquad v(g)= rac{\widetilde v(g)}{\left(\int_{\mathbb D}\widetilde v(g)^2|1+g|^2ight)^{1/2}} \] therefore depends real-analytically on \(g\) in a fixed \(A^2\) neighborhood; the denominator stays uniformly away from zero. Writing \(g=t h\), define \(v_1=Dv(0)[h]\); its forcing has no radial Fourier mode because \(h\) has no constant coefficient. The remaining Taylor terms give \(v^{(2)}+R\), and Cauchy estimates on this fixed neighborhood give the displayed bounds with constants independent of the direction of \(g\).The form identity \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|g|^2|\phi|^2\,dA \le C\|g\|_{A^2}^2\int_{\mathbb D}|
abla\phi|^2\,dA, \qquad \phi\in H^1_0(\mathbb D), \] which follows from Hardy’s inequality, shows that the pulled-back eigenfunction belongs to the weighted Dirichlet space and that the branch is the first Dirichlet branch. Since \(v_0\ge c,d\) and \(\|v-v_0\|_X\le C\sqrt S\), the branch is strictly positive in \(\mathbb D\). This proves the lemma.

By @def-j-functional, \(J(P)=A(P)\lambda_1(P)\); after @def-conformal-data normalizes \(A(P)=\pi(1+S)\), it remains to expand \(\lambda_1(P)\). The fixed-space expansion in @lem-c1-perturbation supplies the uniform eigenpair branch and remainder. For the quantitative rate, write the pulled-back eigenproblem as \[ -\Delta v=\lambda|1+g|^2v,\qquad v|_{\partial\mathbb D}=0, \] with the weighted \(L^2\) normalization. Put \(d(z)=1-|z|\). For \(g\in A^2\) with no constant or linear term, the Bergman pointwise estimate gives \(|g(z)|\le C\|g\|_{A^2}/d(z)\). Consequently, Hardy’s inequality gives, for all \(\varphi,\psi\in H^1_0(\mathbb D)\), \[ \left|\int_{\mathbb D}2\operatorname{Re}(g)\varphi\psiight|\le C\sqrt S\,\|\varphi\|_{H^1_0}\|\psi\|_{H^1_0},\qquad \left|\int_{\mathbb D}|g|^2\varphi\psiight|\le CS\,\|\varphi\|_{H^1_0}\|\psi\|_{H^1_0}. \] Indeed \(|g|^2\le CS/d^2\), \(\int|\varphi|^2/d^2\le4\int|
abla\varphi|^2\), and Cauchy–Schwarz handles the first integral. Therefore the closed forms \[ q_t[\varphi]=\int|
abla\varphi|^2,\qquad m_t[\varphi]=\int|1+t h|^2|\varphi|^2\quad(g=th) \] form a real-analytic type-(a) family on the fixed domain \(H^1_0(\mathbb D)\) for real \(|t|\) small (equivalently, a holomorphic two-parameter family in \((t, ar t)\)), with uniform form bounds. The simple disk eigenvalue is isolated by a fixed spectral gap, so the real-analytic form perturbation theorem applies uniformly to this family.Write \(g=t h\) with \(t=\sqrt S\) and \(\|h\|_{A^2}=1\). The simple disk eigenvalue is isolated by a fixed spectral gap. The form version of analytic simple-eigenvalue perturbation therefore gives, uniformly in such \(h\), \[ v=v_0+t v_1+t^2v_2+O_{H^1_0}(t^3), \qquad \lambda= j^2+t\lambda_1+t^2\lambda_2+O(t^3). \] The case \(S=0\) is the disk and the assertion is immediate, so assume \(S>0\). The first variation is \(\lambda_1=-j^2\int_{\mathbb D}(h+ ar h)v_0^2=0\) because \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient. Write \(v_0(r)=J_0(jr)/(\sqrt\pi J_1(j))\) and \(p_D=j/\sqrt\pi\). For the real mode \(h=a z^n\), the first-order equation in the \(n\)th angular sector has the explicit solution \[ v_1(r,	heta)=a w_n(r)\cos(n	heta),\qquad w_n(r)= rac{r^{n+1}v_0'(r)+p_DJ_n(jr)/J_n(j)}{n+1}. \] The Bessel equation verifies the radial equation and \(w_n(1)=0\). The second-order solvability condition is \[  rac{\lambda_2}{j^2a^2}=-2\pi\int_0^1\left(r^{2n+1}v_0(r)^2+r^{n+1}v_0(r)w_n(r)ight)dr. \] Substitution of \(w_n\) and one integration by parts reduce this to \[  rac{\lambda_2}{j^2a^2}=- rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}, \qquad ho_n=j rac{J_{n+1}(j)}{J_n(j)},\qquad 0<ho_n<2. \] The only nontrivial radial integral is \[ \int_0^1r^{n+1}v_0(r)J_n(jr)\,dr = rac{J_{n+1}(j)}{2\sqrt\pi(n+1)}, \] which follows by one integration by parts from the Bessel equation. Orthogonality of distinct angular modes and density of analytic polynomials extend the formula to every \(h\in A^2\). Since \(A(P)=\pi(1+S)\) in @def-conformal-data, this yields the uniform expansion \[  rac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}). \] The perturbed branch remains the first eigenvalue by the weighted min–max principle: the mass form \(\int|1+g|^2|\varphi|^2\) is positive on nonzero \(H^1_0\) functions, and the branch is the positive continuation of the disk ground state. The sine mode is obtained by a phase rotation, and polarization plus density of analytic polynomials extends the second-order form from real monomials to arbitrary complex \(h\in A^2\). The Bessel interlacing inequalities \(J_n(j)
e0\) and \(0<ho_n<2\) hold for the first zero \(j=j_{0,1}\). Thus \[  rac{\lambda}{j^2}=1-\sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}). \] Multiplying by \(A(P)/(\pi)=1+S\) from @def-conformal-data produces the displayed \(J\) expansion; the cross term \(S\sumho_n|g_n|^2/(n+1)^2\) is \(O(S^2)\) and is absorbed in \(O(S^{3/2})\). Since \(0<ho_n<2\), the quadratic term is at least \(S/3\); after shrinking the universal small neighborhood, \(J(P)/(\pi j^2)-1\ge S/6\). This proves the uniform perturbation expansion and coercivity.

Use the similarity invariance in @def-j-functional to normalize \(A(P)=\pi\) and translate so that the Fraenkel-optimal comparison disk is \(D=B_1(0)\). The regular-polygon asymptotic is \[ \frac{J(R_M)}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{M^3}+O(M^{-5}). \] The upper bound and the displayed asymptotic give \(\lambda_1(P)\le j^2(1+CN^{-3})\), while Faber–Krahn gives \(\lambda_1(P)\ge j^2\). Quantitative Faber–Krahn therefore gives \(|P\triangle D|\to0\). Let \(u_N\) be the normalized positive eigenfunction and extend it by zero. By @lem-uniform-w14, the extensions are uniformly bounded in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) and hence equicontinuous and uniformly bounded. Arzelà–Ascoli gives a locally uniform limit along a subsequence. On every compact set outside \(\overline D\), the limit must vanish: otherwise the uniform Hölder bound would force a fixed positive amount of area in \(P_N\setminus D\), contradicting \(|P_N\triangle D|\to0\). The same argument gives zero trace on \(\partial D\). Since \(\|u_N\|_\infty\) is uniformly bounded, the mass outside \(D\) tends to zero; hence the limit has \(L^2(D)\) norm one. Weak lower semicontinuity gives \(\int_D|\nabla u|^2\le\liminf\lambda_1(P_N)=j^2\), while the disk Rayleigh inequality gives the reverse inequality. Thus the limit is the normalized positive disk eigenfunction \(u_0\). Uniqueness of the limit upgrades the whole sequence to local uniform convergence, and the boundary Hölder bound upgrades it to uniform convergence on \(\overline D\). Since \(u_0>0\) on \(B_{1-\eta}\), eventually \(u_N>0\) there; because the zero extension vanishes off \(P_N\), \(B_{1-\eta}\subset P_N\).The maximal conformal radius is at least \(1-\eta\) by monotonicity under inclusion and at most \(1\) by the conformal area inequality \(A(P)\ge\pi r_P^2\). In the normalization of @def-conformal-data, \(1+S=r_P^{-2}\to1\).By @lem-disk-perturbation, once \(N\) is large enough that \(S\le S_0\), the uniform expansion and coercivity give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}-1\ge S/6. \] The regular-polygon upper bound is \(O(N^{-3})\), hence \(S\le CN^{-3}\) with a universal constant.

If \(S=0\), then \(g=0\) and the assertion is immediate. For \(S>0\), @lem-c1-perturbation gives \[ v=v_0+t v_1+R_2, \qquad \|v_1\|_X\le C, \qquad \|R_2\|_X\le CS, \qquad t=\sqrt S, \] with \(v_1\) having no radial Fourier mode. Separating the angular Fourier modes in the first derivative equation \[ -\Delta v_1-j^2v_1=2j^2\operatorname{Re}(h)v_0 \] and imposing \(v_1|_{\partial\mathbb D}=0\) gives the displayed Bessel solution \(w_n\); the Bessel recurrence gives \(w_n'(1)=-p_Dho_n/(n+1)\). Since \(X\hookrightarrow W^{1,4}(\mathbb D)\) for zero-boundary functions, the claimed \(W^{1,4}\) estimate follows. Set \(b_1=4\,
abla v_0\cdot
abla v_1\,|
abla v_0|^2\); angular orthogonality gives its zero circular mean. The pointwise inequality \[  igl||x+y|^4-|x|^4-4|x|^2x\cdot y igr|\le C(|x|^2|y|^2+|y|^4) \] with \(x=
abla v_0\) and \(y=t
abla v_1+
abla R_2\) gives the stated remainder after separately bounding the omitted linear term \(4|
abla v_0|^2
abla v_0\cdot
abla R_2\) by \(CS\) and using the \(X\) bounds for the quadratic terms.

By @def-conformal-data, \(g\) has no constant coefficient, so \(h\) has no constant coefficient when \(S>0\). Write \(g=th\), \(t=\sqrt S\), and \(\|h\|_{A^2}=1\). By @lem-c1-perturbation, \[ v=v_0+t v_1+e, \qquad \|e\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le CS, \qquad \|v_1\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le C, \] and \(v_1\) has no radial Fourier mode. By @lem-disk-perturbation, \(|\lambda-j^2|\le CS\). Since \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient, angular orthogonality gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}v_0^3v_1\,dA=0, \qquad \int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\operatorname{Re}h\,dA=0. \] The boundedness of \(v_0,v_1,e\) and Cauchy–Schwarz imply \[ v^4=v_0^4+4t v_0^3v_1+E, \qquad \|E\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le CS. \] Multiplying by \(|1+th|^2=1+2t\operatorname{Re}h+t^2|h|^2\) and using \(\|h\|_{L^1}\le C\|h\|_{A^2}\) gives \[ \left|\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA-\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA\right|\le CS. \] Indeed the only terms of order \(t\) are the two displayed zero integrals; all remaining terms contain either \(E\), \(t^2|h|^2\), or the product \(t^2v_0^3v_1\operatorname{Re}h\) and are \(O(S)\). Therefore \[ \lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA =j^4\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA+O(S), \qquad \frac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)}=\frac{j^4}{\pi}+O(S). \] The radial Bessel equation for \(v_0\), integrated by parts using \(v_0(1)=0\) and \(\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^2dA=1\), gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v_0|^4\,dA =j^4\left(\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA-\frac1\pi\right). \] Combining these displays proves the claim.

If \(S=0\) the assertion is immediate. Otherwise write \(g=th\) with \(t=\sqrt S\). By @def-conformal-data, \(k(0)=0\), so the constant coefficient of the analytic function \(k\) is zero and \[ \int_{\mathbb D}a\operatorname{Re}k\,dA=0 \] because \(a\) is radial. The function \(a\) is bounded below on the fixed annulus \(A_0=\{1/2\le|z|\le1\}\). The Bergman pointwise estimate on \(|z|\le1/2\) gives \(|g|\le C\sqrt S\) there, hence \(|k|\le C\sqrt S\) for small \(S\). Thus \[ T\le CS+C\int_{A_0}|k|^2\,dA \le CS+c^{-1}\int_{\mathbb D}a|k|^2\,dA. \] By @lem-gradient-perturbation, \(\|b_1\|_{L^\infty}\le C\) and, from the \(C^1\) remainder used in its proof, \(\|R_1\|_{L^\infty}\le CS\) for \(R_1=|\nabla v|^4-a-tb_1\). Expanding the weighted integral, using the vanishing radial pairing, and applying Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[ \begin{aligned} \int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v|^4|1+k|^2\,dA &\ge \int_{\mathbb D}a\,dA+\int_{\mathbb D}a|k|^2\,dA\\ &\quad-C\bigl(\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+S+S\sqrt T+ST\bigr). \end{aligned} \] The first two errors come from \(t b_1(2\operatorname{Re}k+|k|^2)\), and the remaining ones from \(R_1(1+2\operatorname{Re}k+|k|^2)\). Since \(S\sqrt T\le S+ST\), the preceding control of \(T\) by the \(a|k|^2\) term yields the stated inequality after adjusting \(c,C\).

Under the edge-moment hypotheses @lem-edge-moments, @lem-airy-identity and the conformal change of variables in @def-conformal-data give \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v|^4|1+k|^2 =\lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2- rac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)}. \] By @lem-inverse-left-bound, the left-hand side is at least \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v_0|^4+cT-C\{S+\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+ST\}. \] By @lem-weighted-eigen-balance, the right-hand side is at most \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v_0|^4+CS. \] Comparing these bounds in the identity yields \[ T\le C\{S+\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+ST\}. \] Young’s inequality absorbs the mixed term and, for sufficiently small \(S\), the last two terms, proving \(T\le CS\).

Put \(D=g+k\). Since \(g+k=-gk\) by @def-conformal-data, Hölder gives \[ \|D\|_{A^1}\le \|g\|_{A^2}\|k\|_{A^2}\le CS, \qquad \|D\|_{A^2}^2\le2(S+T)\le CS. \] The constant and linear coefficients of \(D\) vanish. For every \(n\ge2\), the coefficient formula and the two bounds imply \[ |D_n|\le C(n+1)S, \qquad \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{n+1}\le CS. \] With \(K=\lceil S^{-1/2}\rceil\), splitting at \(K\) gives \[ \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{(n+1)^3} \le C S^2\sum_{n\le K}\frac1{n+1} +C(K+1)^{-2}\sum_{n>K}\frac{|D_n|^2}{n+1} \le CS^2\log(e/S). \] Let \(E=k-g\). Since \(|k_n|^2-|g_n|^2=\operatorname{Re}(D_n\overline{E_n})\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[ \left|\sum_{n\ge2}m_n(|k_n|^2-|g_n|^2)\right| \le C C_m \left(\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{(n+1)^3}\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|E_n|^2}{n+1}\right)^{1/2} \le C C_m S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \]Put \(W=L-g\). The scalar estimate \[ |e^z-1-z|\le C\bigl(|e^z-1|^2+|z|^2\bigr) \] and \(e^L-1=g\) give \(\|W\|_{A^1}\le CS\). Also \[ \|L\|_{A^2}^2\le(S+T)/2 \] because \(|e^L|^2+|e^{-L}|^2-2\ge4(\operatorname{Re}L)^2\) pointwise and the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function with zero constant term have equal Bergman energy. Hence \(\|W\|_{A^2}^2\le CS\). The same low/high frequency split gives \[ \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|W_n|^2}{(n+1)^3}\le CS^2\log(e/S). \] Finally \(|L_n|^2-|g_n|^2=\operatorname{Re}(W_n\overline{(L_n+g_n)})\) and \(\sum|L_n+g_n|^2/(n+1)\le CS\), so the second estimate follows by Cauchy–Schwarz.

By @def-conformal-data, \(1+g\) is analytic and nonzero in \(\mathbb D\) with value \(1\) at the origin, so let \(L\) be the analytic logarithm normalized by \(L(0)=0\). Then \(1+g=e^L\) and \((1+g)^{-1}=1+k=e^{-L}\), and the pointwise identity \[ |1+g|^2+|1+k|^2-2 =2\cosh(2\operatorname{Re}L)-2 \ge4(\operatorname{Re}L)^2 \] holds. Integrating and using the definitions of \(S,T\) gives \[ S+T\ge4\|\operatorname{Re}L\|_{A^2}^2. \] The constant coefficient of \(L\) is zero because \((1+g)(0)=1\). For an analytic function with zero constant coefficient, Parseval gives equal Bergman energies for its real and imaginary parts, so \(\|L\|_{A^2}^2=2\|\operatorname{Re}L\|_{A^2}^2\). The displayed inequality follows.

The first-order disk equation in @lem-gradient-perturbation is diagonal in angular Fourier modes. Thus, for \(D=g+k\), \[ M(g,k)-M(g,-g)=\sum_{n\ge2}m_n\operatorname{Re}(g_n\overline{D_n}), \] where \[ m_n=8\pi\int_0^1v_0'(r)^3w_n'(r)r^{n+1}\,dr. \] The explicit Bessel series for \(J_n(jr)/(r^nJ_n(j))\) has denominator bounded away from zero for \(n\ge2\) and derivative \(O((n+1)^{-1})\). The first-order perturbation and the second-order disk calculation from @lem-disk-perturbation give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\rho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}), \] with \(\beta_n=n+1-\rho_n\). By @lem-gradient-perturbation, @lem-inverse-energy and @lem-airy-quadratic-response, \[ S-T=2\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n^2}{(n+1)^2(n^2-1)}|g_n|^2+O\bigl(S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\bigr). \] By @lem-log-energy-bound, \(\|L\|_{A^2}^2\le(S+T)/2\), and by @lem-frequency-replacement every quadratic form with multiplier \(O((n+1)^{-2})\) may replace \(g\) by \(L\) at an error of order \(S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). Combining these facts with the scalar expansion gives \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n}{(n+1)^2}\left(1+\frac{\beta_n}{n^2-1}\right)|L_n|^2-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] Finally @def-turn-measure gives \(L_n=2\widehat\mu(n)/n\), which is the claimed inequality.

Define on \(\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)\) the self-adjoint matrix \[ A_{rs}=\tau^{(r+s)/2}\widehat\mu(r-s)=\sum_iw_i(v_i)_r\overline{(v_i)_s}, \qquad (v_i)_r=\tau^{r/2}e^{-ir\theta_i}. \] The Vandermonde vectors at distinct nodes are linearly independent, so \(A\) has exactly \(p\) positive eigenvalues \(\alpha_1\ge\cdots\ge\alpha_p>0\). The trace is \((1-\tau)^{-1}\), and the negative eigenvalues can only decrease the trace, hence \(Q:=\sum_i\alpha_i\ge(1-\tau)^{-1}\). The shift compression and the min–max principle give \(\alpha_{i+1}\le\tau\alpha_i\). For fixed \(Q\) and these ratio constraints, a finite exchange argument (move mass from an earlier coordinate to the latest coordinate until the active constraint is met) shows that the minimum of the strictly convex function \(\sum_i\alpha_i^2\) is attained at \[ \alpha_i=Q\frac{(1-\tau)\tau^{i-1}}{1-\tau^p},\qquad 1\le i\le p. \] Consequently \[ \sum_i\alpha_i^2\ge Q^2\frac{1-\tau}{1+\tau}\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p} \ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{(1-\tau^2)(1-\tau^p)}. \] On the other hand, \[ \|A\|_{HS}^2=\frac{1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2}{1-\tau^2} \] and the Hilbert–Schmidt norm dominates the squared positive eigenvalues. Rearranging gives \[ 1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2\ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p}, \] which is exactly the claimed bound.

The Bessel bounds \(5.78<j^2<5.8\) give \(1.89<\kappa<1.9\). The recurrence for \(J_n\) implies \(0<\rho_n<2\) and, for \(n\ge3\), \(\rho_n<n\alpha/(n^2+\kappa)\) with \(\alpha=\kappa+1\). Substitution into \[ a_n=\frac{n-\rho_n+\rho_n^2/(n+1)^2}{n^2(n^2-1)} \] proves \(a_n\ge b_n\); for \(n=2\), the identity \(J_0(j)=0\) reduces the inequality to \(\kappa^3+7\kappa^2+12\kappa-54\ge0\), which holds for \(\kappa\ge1.89\).The Laplace representation follows from \[ \int_0^\infty e^{-nt}(1-\cos(\sqrt\kappa t))\,dt=\frac{\kappa}{n(n^2+\kappa)}. \] Apply @lem-toeplitz-positive-atoms with \(\tau=e^{-t}\) and integrate against the nonnegative weight \((1-\cos(\sqrt\kappa t))/\kappa\). Tonelli’s theorem gives \(E_b(\mu)\ge B_p\).

By @lem-spectral-core and @lem-kernel-comparison, \(a_n\ge b_n\) for \(n\ge2\). The missing \(n=1\) term is harmless because @def-turn-measure gives \(\widehat\mu(1)=0\). Hence \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge 1+4E_b(\mu)-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] The lower bound \(E_b(\mu)\ge B_p\) is exactly @lem-kernel-comparison.

If there are at least two reflex corners, the number \(p\) of convex corners is at most \(N-2\). By @lem-near-circle-conformal, \(S\le CN^{-3}\), and @lem-signed-turn-lower-bound gives \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+4B_{N-2}-o(N^{-4}). \] The estimate \(B_p\ge\zeta(3)p^{-3}-\kappa\zeta(5)p^{-5}\) and the regular-polygon asymptotic in @lem-near-circle-conformal imply \[ 4B_{N-2}-\frac{4\zeta(3)}{(N-1)^3}=12\zeta(3)N^{-4}+O(N^{-5})>0 \] for large \(N\), so the assumed upper bound is impossible.

The boundary identity in @def-conformal-data gives a homogeneous \(H^{1/2}\) seminorm of \(F-F(0)-z\) equal to \(S\); restricting it to a straight prevertex arc of length \(\varepsilon\) gives a lower bound \(c\varepsilon^4\), hence every prevertex gap is at most \(CS^{1/4}\). The boundary derivative estimate accompanying @lem-disk-perturbation gives for the disk boundary derivative \(p=-\partial_rv\) on every such arc \[ \operatorname{osc}_I p\le C\{\sqrt S\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(e/\varepsilon)}+S\}\le CS^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \]Place the unique negative turn at angle \(0\). The cotangent formula for \(\ell=\log|F'|\) shows that, on one of the adjacent edges selected according to the sign of the constant term, \(|F'|\) is monotone and the logarithmic drop across a central subarc is at least \(c(a+v)\), where \(-v\) is the reflex weight and \(a\) is the selected adjacent positive weight. For the decreasing function \(h=|F'|\), define \[ \mathsf A=\int_{s<t}h(s)/h(t)\,dsdt,\qquad \mathsf B=\int_{s<t}h(t)/h(s)\,dsdt. \] A four-rectangle comparison gives \[ \frac{\mathsf A-\mathsf B}{\mathsf A+\mathsf B}\ge c(a+v). \] Put \(k_0=h^{-2}\) and normalize the selected edge to \(x\in[0,1]\). The identity equating \(D\) with a first moment of \(k_0\) is not valid for a general monotone \(h\); the needed valid substitute is the following elementary one-dimensional estimate: \[ D=\frac{\int_{s<t}(h(s)/h(t)-h(t)/h(s))\,dsdt}{\int_{s<t}(h(s)/h(t)+h(t)/h(s))\,dsdt},\quad \int_0^1(x-1/2)p(x)^2k_0(x)\,dx=0 \Longrightarrow D\le C\frac{\max_Ip-\min_Ip}{\min_Ip}. \] To verify it, write the numerator and denominator with \(k_0=h^{-2}\), split the square into the four rectangles determined by \(x=1/2\), and use monotonicity of \(k_0\); the centered-moment equation replaces every occurrence of \(\int(x-1/2)k_0\) by \(-\int(x-1/2)(p^2-p_*^2)k_0\), while the denominator is bounded below by the same positive rectangle integrals. Since \(p\ge p_D/2\) uniformly, this gives \(D\le C\operatorname{osc}_I p\). The lower bound \(D\ge c(a+v)\) and the last inequality imply \(a+v\le C S^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). Combining this with \(S\le CN^{-3}\) proves the stated bound.

Let \(\delta=E_b(\mu)-B_{N-1}\ge0\). By @lem-signed-turn-lower-bound, the assumed upper bound and the regular-polygon asymptotic imply \[ \delta\le CN^{-9/2}\sqrt{\log N}. \] For \(U_b(\theta)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_n\operatorname{Re}(\widehat\mu(n)e^{in\theta})\), the Laplace representation in @def-positive-kernel and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[ \|U_b\|_\infty\le C\sqrt\delta+CN^{-5/2}. \] The exact expansion is \[ E_b(\widetilde\mu)-E_b(\mu)= \frac{2a(E_b(\mu)-U_b(\theta_*))+a^2(K_b(0)-E_b(\mu))}{(1-a)^2}, \] where \(K_b(0)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_n\). Since @lem-single-reflex-small-atom gives \(a=O(N^{-9/4}\sqrt{\log N})\) and \(E_b(\mu)=O(N^{-3})\), the right side is \(O(N^{-9/2}\log N)=o(N^{-4})\).

Assume the conclusion fails. If there are at least two reflex corners, @lem-two-reflex-exclusion gives a contradiction. Thus there is exactly one reflex corner. Apply @lem-single-reflex-small-atom and @lem-atom-deletion. The deleted measure has \(N-2\) positive atoms, and @lem-kernel-comparison yields \(E_b(\widetilde\mu)\ge B_{N-2}\). By the proof of @lem-signed-turn-lower-bound (equivalently, by @lem-spectral-core together with @lem-kernel-comparison), \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+4E_b(\mu)-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] Using @lem-atom-deletion and \(S\le CN^{-3}\) from @lem-near-circle-conformal gives \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+4B_{N-2}-o(N^{-4}). \] The regular-polygon asymptotic gives \[ \frac{J(R_{N-1})}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{(N-1)^3}+O(N^{-5}), \] while \(B_{N-2}=\zeta(3)(N-2)^{-3}+O(N^{-5})\). Their difference is \(12\zeta(3)N^{-4}+O(N^{-5})\), contradicting \(J(P)\le J(R_{N-1})\) for large \(N\).

report.summary: The construction is meaningful and defines the stated objects. Finite cyclic deletion terminates, preserves the boundary, and yields a unique maximal straight-segment decomposition; the area is well-defined.

results.statement_text: An admissible polygon is a bounded simple planar polygonal domain whose boundary is a simple cyclic union of finitely many nonzero straight segments, with no self-contact. A genuine corner is a boundary vertex at which the two incident directed segments are not collinear; its interior angle is required to lie strictly between \(0\) and \(2\pi\). Starting from any polygonal presentation, delete adjacent collinear redundant vertices cyclically until no such vertex remains; the resulting effective-edge count is the invariant number \(N\), and \(A(P)\) is the Euclidean area. The cyclic deletion is independent of deletion order because it removes exactly the vertices at which the incoming and outgoing segment directions agree.
results.title: Admissible simple polygon

results.statement_text: For a polygon \(P\) in @def-admissible-polygon, let \(r_P\) be its maximal conformal radius and choose a Riemann map \(F:\mathbb D\to P\) centered at a maximizing point, with \(F'(0)=r_P>0\) and \(F''(0)=0\). The equality \(F''(0)=0\) is the first-order condition for the maximum of \((1-|a|^2)|F'(a)|\). Replace \(P\) by the similarity-normalized polygon \(\widetilde P=r_P^{-1}(P-F(0))\) and write \(\widetilde F=r_P^{-1}(F-F(0))\); by the similarity invariance of \(J\) in @def-j-functional, this leaves \(J\) and the effective-edge count unchanged and gives \(\widetilde F'(0)=1\). In the normalized notation, \[ \widetilde F'(z)=1+g(z),\qquad g(z)=\sum_{n\ge2}g_nz^n. \] Set \[ S=\|g\|_{A^2}^2=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|g_n|^2}{n+1},\qquad T=\|(\widetilde F')^{-1}-1\|_{A^2}^2,\qquad \|h\|_{A^2}^2=\pi^{-1}\int_{\mathbb D}|h|^2dA. \] The area identity is \(A(\widetilde P)=\pi(1+S)\); all later uses of \(P,F,A,\lambda_1\) are understood in this similarity-normalized representative. Write \(k=(\widetilde F')^{-1}-1\), so \(T=\|k\|_{A^2}^2\) and \(g+k=-gk\). The inverse derivative is in \(A^2\): at a prevertex with interior angle \(\omega\in(0,2\pi)\), the Schwarz–Christoffel exponent is \(\alpha=\omega/\pi-1<1\), so \(|(\widetilde F')^{-1}|^2=O(r^{-2\alpha})\) and its area integral is bounded by \(C\int_0^\varepsilon r^{1-2\alpha}\,dr<\infty\).

results.statement_text: For an admissible polygon \(P\) in @def-admissible-polygon, let \(\lambda_1(P)\) be the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of \(-\Delta\) on the bounded nondegenerate polygonal domain \(P\) and define \[ J(P)=A(P)\lambda_1(P),\qquad m_k=\inf\{J(Q):Q\text{ is admissible and has at most }k\text{ effective edges}\}. \] Here \(k\ge3\) is an integer, and \(R_k\) denotes the unit-area regular \(k\)-gon (its position is irrelevant because \(J\) is similarity invariant). The first eigenvalue is defined by the Dirichlet Rayleigh quotient on \(H_0^1(P)\).

results.statement_text: Let \(j=j_{0,1}\) be the first positive zero of the Bessel function \(J_0\), let \(\kappa=j^2/2-1>0\), and define for \(n\ge1\) \[ b_n=\frac1{n(n^2+\kappa)},\qquad E_b(\mu)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2, \] for a finite real atomic measure \(\mu\) of total mass \(1\) as in @def-turn-measure. results.statement_text: An admissible polygon in @def-admissible-polygon, with \(J\) as defined in @def-j-functional, is stationary when, in a differentiable local chart of its effective vertex coordinates, \(DJ(P)[V]=0\) for every vertex variation \(V\). On the same chart this is equivalent to \(D\lambda_1(P)[V]=0\) for every variation with \(DA(P)[V]=0\): the forward implication follows from \(DJ=A\,D\lambda_1+\lambda_1\,DA\), and the converse follows by applying the scaling identities \(D\lambda_1[X]=-2\lambda_1\) and \(DA[X]=2A\) to the radial variation and then using the Lagrange-multiplier decomposition.

Direct multiplication gives \[ H_2(g,k)=\pi p_D^4(T-S)+Q_0(g)+A(k)+M(g,k), \] where \(A(k)=\int(a-p_D^4)|k|^2dA\) and \(M(g,k)=2\int b_1(g)\operatorname{Re}k\,dA\); \(Q_0\) contains the remaining pure quadratic terms in \(v(g)\), \(\lambda(g)\) and \(g\).For the quadratic part, the radial term \(A(k)\) has coefficients \(O((n+1)^{-2})\) by \(|a(r)-p_D^4|\le C(1-r)\). By @def-conformal-data, \(g\) is analytic, has no constant or linear coefficient, and satisfies \(S=\|g\|_{A^2}^2\); its normalized conformal pullback is the weighted disk problem used below. Put \(d(z)=1-|z|\). The Green kernel of the disk satisfies \[ |

abla_xG_D(x,z)|\le C rac{d(z)}{|x-z|^2}. \] The Bergman pointwise estimate gives \(|g(z)|\le C\|g\|_{A^2}/d(z)\) for \(g\in A^2\) with vanishing constant coefficient. If \(h\in X\), then \(|h(z)|\le d(z)\|h\|_X\). Splitting the Green integral into \(|x-z|<d(x)/2\), the annulus \(d(x)/2\le|x-z|<2d(x)\), and dyadic outer annuli, the two kernel bounds give \[ \|G_D(gh)\|_X\le C\|g\|_{A^2}\|h\|_X, \qquad \|G_D(g_1\overline{g_2}h)\|_X\le C\|g_1\|_{A^2}\|g_2\|_{A^2}\|h\|_X. \] For example, in the near region \(d(z)\simeq d(x)\) and the pointwise bounds leave an integrable \(|x-z|^{-1}\) kernel; in the outer annuli \(d(z)\le d(x)+|x-z|\) cancels one power of the second Green bound, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\|g_1g_2\|_{L^1}\le C\|g_1\|_{A^2}\|g_2\|_{A^2}\). Polynomial approximation extends these estimates to all \(A^2\) data, and the Green potential has a continuous boundary derivative.Define the real quadratic compact-operator family \[ K_g h=G_D[|1+g|^2h]=G_D[h+2\operatorname{Re}(g)h+|g|^2h] \] onlinearly in \(g\). The estimates give \(\|K_g-K_0\|_{B(X)}\le C(\sqrt S+S)\). The operator \(K_0\) is compact on \(X\) by disk Poisson regularity and the compact embedding \(C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{\mathbb D})\Subset C^1(\overline{\mathbb D})\). Its nonzero eigenvalues are the reciprocals of the Dirichlet eigenvalues; \(1/j^2\) is an isolated simple eigenvalue.Choose a fixed small contour \(\Gamma\) enclosing only \(1/j^2\). For \(S\) small, the Neumann series uniformly bounds \((zI-K_g)^{-1}\) on \(\Gamma\) and defines the rank-one Riesz projection \[ \Pi_g= rac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma(zI-K_g)^{-1}\,dz. \] The normalized vector \[ \widetilde v(g)=\Pi_gv_0, \qquad v(g)= rac{\widetilde v(g)}{\left(\int_{\mathbb D}\widetilde v(g)^2|1+g|^2ight)^{1/2}} \] therefore depends real-analytically on \(g\) in a fixed \(A^2\) neighborhood; the denominator stays uniformly away from zero. Writing \(g=t h\), define \(v_1=Dv(0)[h]\); its forcing has no radial Fourier mode because \(h\) has no constant coefficient. abla\phi|^2\,dA, \qquad \phi\in H^1_0(\mathbb D), \] which follows from Hardy’s inequality, shows that the pulled-back eigenfunction belongs to the weighted Dirichlet space and that the branch is the first Dirichlet branch. Since \(v_0\ge c,d\) and \(\|v-v_0\|_X\le C\sqrt S\), the branch is strictly positive in \(\mathbb D\). This proves the lemma.

results.proof_text: By @def-stationary-polygon, the derivative of \(J=A\lambda\) vanishes for every vertex displacement. Hadamard’s formula is \[ DJ[V]=A\int_{\partial P}(c-q)V\cdot\nu\,ds. \] Moving one endpoint of an effective edge while keeping the other fixed produces an affine normal velocity on that edge, and the two endpoint velocities give the independent functions \(1\) and \(s/\ell_E\). Since adjacent effective edge normals are linearly independent at a genuine corner, stationarity forces both coefficients of these two affine test functions to vanish. Rescaling \(s/\ell_E\) gives the displayed moments.

results.proof_text: Use the similarity invariance in @def-j-functional to normalize \(A(P)=\pi\) and translate so that the Fraenkel-optimal comparison disk is \(D=B_1(0)\). The regular-polygon asymptotic is \[ \frac{J(R_M)}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{M^3}+O(M^{-5}). \] The upper bound and the displayed asymptotic give \(\lambda_1(P)\le j^2(1+CN^{-3})\), while Faber–Krahn gives \(\lambda_1(P)\ge j^2\). Quantitative Faber–Krahn therefore gives \(|P\triangle D|\to0\). Let \(u_N\) be the normalized positive eigenfunction and extend it by zero. By @lem-uniform-w14, the extensions are uniformly bounded in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) and hence equicontinuous and uniformly bounded. Arzelà–Ascoli gives a locally uniform limit along a subsequence. On every compact set outside \(\overline D\), the limit must vanish: otherwise the uniform Hölder bound would force a fixed positive amount of area in \(P_N\setminus D\), contradicting \(|P_N\triangle D|\to0\). The same argument gives zero trace on \(\partial D\). Since \(\|u_N\|_\infty\) is uniformly bounded, the mass outside \(D\) tends to zero; hence the limit has \(L^2(D)\) norm one. Weak lower semicontinuity gives \(\int_D|\nabla u|^2\le\liminf\lambda_1(P_N)=j^2\), while the disk Rayleigh inequality gives the reverse inequality. Thus the limit is the normalized positive disk eigenfunction \(u_0\). Uniqueness of the limit upgrades the whole sequence to local uniform convergence, and the boundary Hölder bound upgrades it to uniform convergence on \(\overline D\). Since \(u_0>0\) on \(B_{1-\eta}\), eventually \(u_N>0\) there; because the zero extension vanishes off \(P_N\), \(B_{1-\eta}\subset P_N\).The maximal conformal radius is at least \(1-\eta\) by monotonicity under inclusion and at most \(1\) by the conformal area inequality \(A(P)\ge\pi r_P^2\). In the normalization of @def-conformal-data, \(1+S=r_P^{-2}\to1\).By @lem-disk-perturbation, once \(N\) is large enough that \(S\le S_0\), the uniform expansion and coercivity give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}-1\ge S/6. \] The regular-polygon upper bound is \(O(N^{-3})\), hence \(S\le CN^{-3}\) with a universal constant.

results.proof_text: The boundary identity in @def-conformal-data gives a homogeneous \(H^{1/2}\) seminorm of \(F-F(0)-z\) equal to \(S\); restricting it to a straight prevertex arc of length \(\varepsilon\) gives a lower bound \(c\varepsilon^4\), hence every prevertex gap is at most \(CS^{1/4}\). The boundary derivative estimate accompanying @lem-disk-perturbation gives for the disk boundary derivative \(p=-\partial_rv\) on every such arc \[ \operatorname{osc}_I p\le C\{\sqrt S\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(e/\varepsilon)}+S\}\le CS^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \]Place the unique negative turn at angle \(0\). The cotangent formula for \(\ell=\log|F'|\) shows that, on one of the adjacent edges selected according to the sign of the constant term, \(|F'|\) is monotone and the logarithmic drop across a central subarc is at least \(c(a+v)\), where \(-v\) is the reflex weight and \(a\) is the selected adjacent positive weight. For the decreasing function \(h=|F'|\), define \[ \mathsf A=\int_{s<t}h(s)/h(t)\,dsdt,\qquad \mathsf B=\int_{s<t}h(t)/h(s)\,dsdt. \] A four-rectangle comparison gives \[ \frac{\mathsf A-\mathsf B}{\mathsf A+\mathsf B}\ge c(a+v). \] Put \(k_0=h^{-2}\) and normalize the selected edge to \(x\in[0,1]\). The identity equating \(D\) with a first moment of \(k_0\) is not valid for a general monotone \(h\); the needed valid substitute is the following elementary one-dimensional estimate: \[ D=\frac{\int_{s<t}(h(s)/h(t)-h(t)/h(s))\,dsdt}{\int_{s<t}(h(s)/h(t)+h(t)/h(s))\,dsdt},\quad \int_0^1(x-1/2)p(x)^2k_0(x)\,dx=0 \Longrightarrow D\le C\frac{\max_Ip-\min_Ip}{\min_Ip}. \] To verify it, write the numerator and denominator with \(k_0=h^{-2}\), split the square into the four rectangles determined by \(x=1/2\), and use monotonicity of \(k_0\); the centered-moment equation replaces every occurrence of \(\int(x-1/2)k_0\) by \(-\int(x-1/2)(p^2-p_*^2)k_0\), while the denominator is bounded below by the same positive rectangle integrals. Since \(p\ge p_D/2\) uniformly, this gives \(D\le C\operatorname{osc}_I p\). The lower bound \(D\ge c(a+v)\) and the last inequality imply \(a+v\le C S^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). Combining this with \(S\le CN^{-3}\) proves the stated bound.

results.proof_text: Define on \(\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)\) the self-adjoint matrix \[ A_{rs}=\tau^{(r+s)/2}\widehat\mu(r-s)=\sum_iw_i(v_i)_r\overline{(v_i)_s}, \qquad (v_i)_r=\tau^{r/2}e^{-ir\theta_i}. \] The Vandermonde vectors at distinct nodes are linearly independent, so \(A\) has exactly \(p\) positive eigenvalues \(\alpha_1\ge\cdots\ge\alpha_p>0\). The trace is \((1-\tau)^{-1}\), and the negative eigenvalues can only decrease the trace, hence \(Q:=\sum_i\alpha_i\ge(1-\tau)^{-1}\). The shift compression and the min–max principle give \(\alpha_{i+1}\le\tau\alpha_i\). For fixed \(Q\) and these ratio constraints, a finite exchange argument (move mass from an earlier coordinate to the latest coordinate until the active constraint is met) shows that the minimum of the strictly convex function \(\sum_i\alpha_i^2\) is attained at \[ \alpha_i=Q\frac{(1-\tau)\tau^{i-1}}{1-\tau^p},\qquad 1\le i\le p. \] Consequently \[ \sum_i\alpha_i^2\ge Q^2\frac{1-\tau}{1+\tau}\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p} \ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{(1-\tau^2)(1-\tau^p)}. \] On the other hand, \[ \|A\|_{HS}^2=\frac{1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2}{1-\tau^2} \] and the Hilbert–Schmidt norm dominates the squared positive eigenvalues. Rearranging gives \[ 1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2\ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p}, \] which is exactly the claimed bound.
results.statement_text: Let \(\mu\) be a finite real atomic measure of total mass \(1\) with exactly \(p\) positive atoms, allowing arbitrary negative atoms. For \(0<\tau<1\), \[ \sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2\ge\frac{\tau^p}{1-\tau^p}. \]

Under the edge-moment hypotheses, @lem-airy-identity applies, and \(\int_Pu^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\int_Pu^2=\|u\|_\infty^2\); combining these facts yields \[ \int_P|\nabla u|^4\le \frac{e^2\lambda^3}{8\pi}. \] The same \(L^\infty\) bound gives \(\int_P|u|^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\), so the \(W^{1,4}(P)\) norm is bounded by a constant depending only on \(A_0\) and \(\Lambda\). Since \(u\in H^1_0(P)\), its zero extension has no boundary distribution term in its weak gradient; the extension therefore lies in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) with the same gradient bound. Morrey’s inequality in dimension two then gives a \(C^{0,1/2}\) representative with the same parameter dependence.

results.proof_text: By @def-conformal-data, \(g\) has no constant coefficient, so \(h\) has no constant coefficient when \(S>0\). Write \(g=th\), \(t=\sqrt S\), and \(\|h\|_{A^2}=1\). By @lem-c1-perturbation, \[ v=v_0+t v_1+e, \qquad \|e\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le CS, \qquad \|v_1\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le C, \] and \(v_1\) has no radial Fourier mode. By @lem-disk-perturbation, \(|\lambda-j^2|\le CS\). Since \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient, angular orthogonality gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}v_0^3v_1\,dA=0, \qquad \int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\operatorname{Re}h\,dA=0. \] The boundedness of \(v_0,v_1,e\) and Cauchy–Schwarz imply \[ v^4=v_0^4+4t v_0^3v_1+E, \qquad \|E\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le CS. \] Multiplying by \(|1+th|^2=1+2t\operatorname{Re}h+t^2|h|^2\) and using \(\|h\|_{L^1}\le C\|h\|_{A^2}\) gives \[ \left|\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA-\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA\right|\le CS. \] Indeed the only terms of order \(t\) are the two displayed zero integrals; all remaining terms contain either \(E\), \(t^2|h|^2\), or the product \(t^2v_0^3v_1\operatorname{Re}h\) and are \(O(S)\). Therefore \[ \lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA =j^4\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA+O(S), \qquad \frac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)}=\frac{j^4}{\pi}+O(S). \] The radial Bessel equation for \(v_0\), integrated by parts using \(v_0(1)=0\) and \(\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^2dA=1\), gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v_0|^4\,dA =j^4\left(\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA-\frac1\pi\right). \] Combining these displays proves the claim.
results.statement_text: For normalized conformal data in @def-conformal-data with \(S\) sufficiently small, let \(v\) and \(\lambda\) be the positive weighted first eigenpair in @lem-disk-perturbation, and let \(v_0(r)=J_0(jr)/(\sqrt\pi J_1(j))\). Then \[ \left|\lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA- \frac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)}- \int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v_0|^4\,dA\right|\le CS. \] The constant is universal.

results.proof_text: Assume the conclusion fails. If there are at least two reflex corners, @lem-two-reflex-exclusion gives a contradiction. Thus there is exactly one reflex corner. Apply @lem-single-reflex-small-atom and @lem-atom-deletion. The deleted measure has \(N-2\) positive atoms, and @lem-kernel-comparison yields \(E_b(\widetilde\mu)\ge B_{N-2}\). By the proof of @lem-signed-turn-lower-bound (equivalently, by @lem-spectral-core together with @lem-kernel-comparison), \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+4E_b(\mu)-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] Using @lem-atom-deletion and \(S\le CN^{-3}\) from @lem-near-circle-conformal gives \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+4B_{N-2}-o(N^{-4}). \] The regular-polygon asymptotic gives \[ \frac{J(R_{N-1})}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{(N-1)^3}+O(N^{-5}), \] while \(B_{N-2}=\zeta(3)(N-2)^{-3}+O(N^{-5})\). Their difference is \(12\zeta(3)N^{-4}+O(N^{-5})\), contradicting \(J(P)\le J(R_{N-1})\) for large \(N\).
results.statement_text: There is a universal \(N_0\) such that, for every \(N\ge N_0\), every admissible stationary simple \(N\)-gon \(P\) satisfying \[ J(P)\le J(R_{N-1}) \] is convex. Consequently, no such polygon satisfies \(J(P)<m_{N-1}\) while being non-convex.
results.title: Large-N low-threshold stationary polygons are convex
